preamble: In Portuguese the falling diphthong ou [ow], mostly from Latin au (causa > cousa, aurum > ouro) and from vocalized l, was replaced by oi [oj] in many words from the late Middle Ages on. Some of these became standard (cousa > coisa 'thing', dous > dois 'two', with cousa and dous now dated), while others survive as variants (ouro ~ oiro 'gold', touro ~ toiro 'bull'). The change spread word by word rather than as a regular sound law, and its cause is debated: E. B. Williams traces it to interdialectal confusion after Latin -oct- gave both -oit- and -out-, Maia and Moffat to confusion of the suffixes -ouro (< -auru) and -doiro (< -toriu), and Cintra to 'vocalic differentiation' in central Portugal, the transition zone where [ow] is being monophthongized to [o]. Today [oj] is most frequent between the Douro and the Tejo. Fala, the Galician-Portuguese variety of the Xálima valley in Spain, shows the same oi outcome in oiru 'gold', toiru 'bull' and dois 'two'.

examples.note: The oi form is now standard in both Portugal and Brazil; cousa is dated.
The oi form is standard; dous is dated.
Alternative form; in mainland Portugal ou and oi alternate in word-initial and word-medial position, with oi most frequent in central Portugal.
